Photograph: Chema Moya/EPA View image in fullscreen Spain's prime minister Pedro Sánchez is one of the few European leaders who seems to be taking the climate crisis seriously. Photograph: Chema Moya/EPA This Is Europe World news ​W​hy are European leaders staying silent after our summer of climate shock? Lethal temperatures ​and wildfires have exposed a widening gulf between voters demanding ​action and politicians unwilling to confront the long-term choices global heating requires Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Jon Henley Wed 26 Aug 2026 10.40 EDT Last modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 10.41 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T he climate crisis means “we’re going to have to change everything – the way we live, the way we produce, the way we trade,” France’s veteran radical-left firebrand, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, told the summer congress of his France Insoumise party last weekend. The term “climate change”, said Mélenchon – the most likely rival to Marine Le Pen in next year’s presidential run-off, according to one poll this week – may sound “almost reassuring”, but its actual impact will feel like “landing on another planet whenever we leave home”. The speech is notable because despite the four heatwaves that have scorched Europe this summer, shattering temperature records , fanning unprecedented fires and causing thousands of excess deaths , few politicians want to talk about climate action. Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent , heating up twice as quickly as elsewhere. The consequences, as UN climate chief Simon Stiell puts it, are “reaching national emergency levels”. And yet major policy speeches by Europe’s political leaders addressing the climate crisis, making plain its causes, and laying out the changes that will be needed to live with it can be counted on the fingers of one hand. French voters have faced “silence from some politicians and inadequate pronouncements or demagoguery from others”, said Le Monde in a stark editorial , warning that “decision-makers on both the right and the left are losing credibility”. People want “a political message that translates into action, and sheds light on the future”, it said. The gap between “citizens’ heightened awareness of the crisis and the lack of commitment from their elected officials to address it” will trigger mounting frustration and anger. A mid-July Ipsos poll found environmental protection had jumped 12 points from June to become French voters’ fourth greatest concern, after what the pollster described as “a first real experience of what the hell of a significantly hotter world might look like”. In the UK too, Labour party activists worry that despite the ever more visible impacts of the climate crisis, there has been no major political push from the government on the issue, even as voters become increasingly convinced of the need for action. And while Friedrich Merz said this week action was needed to “curb climate change and adapt to the consequences” (though not at a cost to German industry), he’s been accused all summer of ducking the issue for fear of boosting the climate-sceptic, far-right AfD . There are, of course, exceptions. Spain’s outspoken prime minister, Pedro Sánchez (pictured top), has long warned that “climate change kills”, and recently stressed: “It’s not enough to address the consequences; what we have to do is reduce its causes.” A French centre-left presidential contender, Raphäel Glucksmann, spoke this week of the need for an “ecological transformation” ending the use of fossil fuels, and pledged a 100-day “ecological revolution” if elected president (which looks extremely unlikely). But the silence from most mainstream politicians is deafening, says Jean Jouzel , a veteran French climatologist. The political class in general, he says, “have simply not yet engaged with the reality of global heating. They have to tackle it head-on.” The root of the problem, Jouzel suggests, is that “politicians live in the short-term. Their horizon is avoiding any damage during their period in office. For me, a real political leader … has the courage to look to the medium and the long-term.” Short-termism, political polarisation and cost-of-living fears have, in effect, silenced leaders across Europe, as populist and far-right parties successfully frame green laws as an “ideological mantra” and the elite’s punishment for “ordinary working people”. The reasoning is clear: voters suffering high energy bills, food inflation and stagnating wages are unlikely to hail demands for real financial and lifestyle sacrifices in pursuit of an ill-defined climate gain. Carbon taxes and boiler restrictions carry electoral risk. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Local over global View image in fullscreen The summer heatdome over Europe caused an unprecedented demand for air conditioners – for those who can afford them. Photograph: Cristina Quicler/AFP/Getty Images But that reluctance to address the real issue has shifted Europe’s climate debate away from long-term carbon reduction towards more localised adaptation – which, perhaps inevitably, has itself now become a battleground in the continent’s culture wars . Air conditioning is a prime example, now loudly touted on Europe’s right as a vital symbol of personal freedom and technological comfort, but widely decried by the left as environmentally irresponsible and symptomatic of long-term planning failures. “If I am elected president, I will put into place a massive air-conditioning plan,” Le Pen trumpeted this summer , arguing the technology had little or no impact on global heating: “When environmentalists don’t want something, they twist the studies.” The risk in all this is that by focusing on necessary but essentially reactive coping measures, leaders wind up reducing the existential challenges of global heating to debates over consumer choice and comfort that can fit into an electoral cycle. Meanwhile, vital long-term carbon reduction gets pushed further and further into the background. As Dutch MEP, Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy , argues: “Nobody should feel guilty for wanting relief from extreme heat. Air conditioning saves lives.” However, he continues, neither should we “accept the cynical argument that the answer to rising temperatures is simply to install more air conditioning – while abandoning the very policies designed to tackle the causes of those rising temperatures”. Be that as it may, in the multiple European countries with national elections coming up over the next 18 months – including France, Italy and Spain – the climate emergency remains, for the time being at least, largely absent from the debate. And that’s regrettable, because as Jouzel says: “Global heating is no longer a scientific debate. It’s a very real political problem.” Grégoire Leménager , writing in the French weekly Le Nouvel Obs, agreed. “Looking the other way is no longer an option,” he said. Nothing is simple, but after the summer Europe has just endured, politicians who “refuse to make climate action a cornerstone of their manifestos” will, he continued, “be exposed for what they are: criminal accomplices to an inevitable defeat”. (Image: Mayflower) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. Rehearsal images have been released for the world premiere of a musical adaptation of The Pianist . The stage adaptation of Wladyslaw Szpilman’s memoir, starring Daniel Krikler, will debut at Mayflower Studios. The production, directed by Thom Southerland, will run from September 9 to 12. Szpilman’s compositions, along with new arrangements by Simon Lee, will be showcased in the musical. The cast, including Rosalind Ford, Oliver Grant, and TJ Holmes, will bring to life the essence of Jewish Warsaw. READ MORE: Mayflower Studios announces Shout Season to return The production, produced by Wolk Transfer Company and Willette Klausner, with Szpilman’s son Andreas Szpilman, aims to celebrate the enduring power of creativity. The creative team is led by adaptor and director Thom Southerland. New lyrics by international writers and musicians, including Carol Connors and Szpilman’s son, will feature in the production. The Pianist will showcase Szpilman’s legacy as a Holocaust survivor, composer, and pianist. Tickets are available on Mayflower's website. https://www.baltictimes.com/nordic_inves.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Nordic Investment Bank chooses Origo One, reinforcing the Riga Central Business District as an international financial hub 2026-09-29 The Nordic Investment Bank (NIB) has signed a long-term lease agreement with the Origo One Class A office complex for 210 m² of office space. NIB's relocation to larger premises at Origo One reflects the continued growth of the Bank's activities across the Baltic region and further reinforces the Riga Central Business District's position as a leading centre for business and finance in the Baltics. Its central location provides excellent access to both business infrastructure and major transport connections, making it an ideal choice for forward-looking organisations. The new office at Origo One will provide NIB with a modern, sustainable workplace designed to the highest international standards, located in the heart of Riga, adjacent to the city's main public transport hub and the future Rail Baltica Central Station. "NIB's decision to choose Origo One is a significant endorsement of the Riga Central Business District's growing position as an internationally competitive business and financial destination. More and more international companies and financial institutions are prioritising sustainable infrastructure, premium-quality work environments and strategically located office space. The arrival of organisations such as NIB not only strengthens Origo One's position as a Class A office complex but also contributes to the continued development of the Riga Central Business District as one of the Baltics' leading business and financial centres," says Evija Majevska, Commercial Director of Linstow Baltic and Origo multifunctional centre. “The opening of NIB's Riga office in 2023 was an important milestone in bringing the Bank closer to its Baltic owners, clients and partners. As our activities and engagement across the region have continued to grow, the relocation to larger premises marks the next step in the development of our Baltic hub. The new office will support closer collaboration with stakeholders and help advance investments that contribute to a resilient, sustainable and competitive Nordic-Baltic region,” says Jukka Ahonen, Chief Corporate Affairs Officer at NIB. NIB is the international financial institution of Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, and Sweden. The Bank strengthens the competitiveness, sustainability, and resilience of the Nordic-Baltic region. By choosing Origo One, NIB joins a growing community of international companies and organisations that have established their operations in the Riga Central Business District. The 11,500 m² Origo One business centre is a Class A office centre strategically located in Riga’s Central Business District, adjacent to the city’s key transport and commercial infrastructure, including Riga Central Railway Station, Riga International Bus Station, the Old Town, shopping centres, banks and hotels. In addition, significant transport infrastructure improvements are underway in the area, including the implementation of the Rail Baltica project. The direct connection to the Origo shopping centre provides access to a wide range of dining, retail and everyday services. This infrastructure is a key advantage of Origo One for companies seeking to offer their teams a convenient and well-rounded working environment in the very heart of Riga. In spring 2021, Origo One obtained the world’s leading building sustainability assessment method’s BREEAM certification in the spring of 2021, gaining the highest final rating “Excellent” among all business centres in Latvia at that time. The project emphasizes high standards of energy efficiency, working environment and sustainability to, with the help of nature and environmentally friendly solutions, provide a healthy and comfortable environment for office workers and visitors alike. The Origo One business centre offers Class A modern, functional, and flexible office spaces that meet current market requirements and the needs of businesses. The building is equipped with the latest technologies and eco-friendly solutions that promote energy efficiency and sustainable development. For tenant convenience, there is a spacious underground parking lot with 130 spaces, including electric vehicle charging stations, as well as a bicycle parking area with a self-service repair station. Companies such as Reitan Convenience Latvia (Narvesen and Caffeine), Preses Serviss, Colliers International, LETA, TVNET Group, Entain NCE, RB Rail AS, VGP Industrial Development Latvia and LAFI Serviss have already established their offices at the Origo One business centre. About “Origo One” The 11,500 m² Origo One business centre is a Class A office centre located in “Riga’s Central Business District”, offering direct access to key urban and international transport connections. Opened in 2020, “Origo One” provides a sustainable, high-quality working environment with flexible layouts, modern technologies, and well-developed infrastructure for employee convenience – including 248 parking spaces, EV charging stations, bicycle storage, and landscaped outdoor areas. In 2021, the building received a BREEAM “Excellent” certification with the highest rating in Latvia and was awarded 1st place in the “Latvian Construction Annual Award” as the Best New Public Building. Origo One’s tenant portfolio includes Reitan Convenience Latvia (Narvesen and Caffeine), Preses Serviss, Colliers International, LETA, TVNET Group, Entain NCE, RB Rail AS, VGP Industrial Development Latvia and LAFI Serviss. For more information: www.origoone.lv About Linstow Baltic (LB) Linstow Baltic is a leading developer of long-term real estate projects across various segments, including office buildings, shopping centres, hotels, parking facilities, and more, in the Baltic region. LB has been operating in this sector since 1996. In Latvia, it manages and develops the Origo shopping centre and the largest shopping centre in Estonia, Ülemiste. In the centre of Riga, LB manages the modern, environmentally and socially responsible ‘Origo One’ business centre, as well as developing the dynamic city quarter SPORTA 2 and the sustainable business complex SATEKLES BUSINESS CENTRE. Linstow Baltic does not offer real estate transaction intermediary services. For more information: www.linstowbaltic.lv .
